edges.description: Human egg ingestion is upstream of the liver metacestode lesion that expands as the active parasite mass.
edges.source: Egg Ingestion and Hepatic Larval Establishment

edges.description: The intrahepatic metacestode mass is the lesion detected by ultrasound, CT, and MRI.
Viable metacestodes are surrounded by a host immune infiltrate that constrains, tolerates, and helps wall off the parasite.
Local infiltrative growth reaches central bile ducts and can obstruct biliary drainage.
Local infiltrative growth reaches the portal vein, hepatic veins, and inferior vena cava.
Locally advanced lesions can extend from the liver into adjacent organs.
Advanced lesions can seed distant organs through hematogenous spread.
A late excessive Th1/Th2 host response walls off the lesion with periparasitic fibrosis.
Biliary involvement can present as painless jaundice.
Chronic alveolar-echinococcosis obstruction of central bile ducts causes secondary biliary sclerosis and can progress to cirrhosis.
edges.target: Recurrent Biliary Obstruction and Secondary Biliary Sclerosis

edges.description: Portal-vein compression or thrombosis, hepatic-vein or vena-cava obstruction, and cirrhosis can converge on portal hypertension.
Infiltration of hepatic venous drainage can produce chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome.
Neighboring-organ involvement produces extrahepatic lesions tracked in PNM staging.
Distant spread produces extrahepatic lesions tracked in PNM staging.
The lung is the most common distant site of metastasis-like AE spread.
Impaired protective immunity shifts the periparasitic host response toward weaker metacestode control, permitting faster growth and spread.

edges.source: Ex vivo liver resection and autotransplantation
Repeated ERCP with balloon dilatation or stenting
edges.target: Recurrent Biliary Obstruction and Secondary Biliary Sclerosis

nodes.description: Benzimidazoles, chiefly albendazole or mebendazole, are the recommended parasitostatic drugs for AE. They are used after complete resection to prevent relapse and as long-term or lifelong suppression in inoperable disease.

evidence.reference_title: Chemotherapy for the treatment of alveolar echinococcosis: Where are we?
evidence.snippet: Benzimidazoles are the only compounds recommended for the treatment of AE; however, these are parasitostatic, which means that the parasite can resume growth when treatment is interrupted.

nodes.description: Central infiltration and compression of bile ducts drive painless jaundice, recurrent or chronic obstruction, cholangitis risk, and secondary biliary sclerosis.

evidence.snippet: Painless jaundice is a sign of infiltration of the liver hilum and central biliary vessel involvement.
Alveolar echinococcosis-related recurrent and chronic biliary obstruction leads to secondary biliary sclerosis and ultimately cirrhosis

nodes.description: Infiltration of the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava can obstruct hepatic venous outflow and produce chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Alveolar echinococcosis-related infiltration of the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava causes chronic Budd–Chiari syndrome and progressive damage to liver tissue and liver cirrhosis.

nodes.description: Advanced hepatic lesions can directly infiltrate neighboring organs, the N domain in the WHO-IWGE PNM staging system.

evidence.snippet: It describes the extension of the parasitic mass in the liver (P), the involvement of neighboring organs (N) and metastases (M)

nodes.description: Ingested eggs establish the human hepatic E. multilocularis metacestode stage that drives alveolar echinococcosis.
nodes.id: Egg Ingestion and Hepatic Larval Establishment

evidence.reference_title: Chemotherapy for the treatment of alveolar echinococcosis: Where are we?
evidence.snippet: Humans, as aberrant intermediate hosts, become infected by ingesting eggs through contaminated water, food or hands.

nodes.description: ELRA removes the liver for back-table lesion resection and reconstruction before autotransplanting the remnant, extending radical surgery to selected advanced AE with portal, hepatic-vein, caval, arterial, or biliary involvement, including end-stage lesions and Budd-Chiari presentations.
nodes.id: Ex vivo liver resection and autotransplantation

evidence.reference_title: Alveolar Echinococcosis in the Early 2020s: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: ex vivo liver resection and autotransplantation (ELRA), where a significant portion of the liver is extracted, lesion resection is performed, and then the remaining tissue is autotransplanted back into the patient

evidence.reference_title: Alveolar Echinococcosis in the Early 2020s: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: Generally, ELRA is indicated for patients with lesions extending towards the portal vein, hepatic veins, and/or arteries (P4 on the PNM scale), with or without neighboring organ invasion (N0 or N1) and metastases (M0 or M1)

nodes.description: In later disease, hematogenous dissemination can establish distant metastasis-like AE lesions, most often in the lung and less often in the brain, bone, or other sites.

evidence.reference_title: The Echinococcoses: Diagnosis, Clinical Management and Burden of Disease.
evidence.snippet: clinical manifestations associated with AE resemble those of a 'malignant', silently-progressing liver disease, with local tissue infiltration and metastases.

evidence.reference_title: Alveolar Echinococcosis in the Early 2020s: A Systematic Review.
evidence.snippet: In later stages of infection, the parasitic lesion may spread through the hematogenous dissemination of protoscoleces to other organs, with the most common secondary sites of infection being the lung and brain

nodes.description: Therapeutic or pathologic immunosuppression increases the chance that exposure progresses to active AE and accelerates growth and metastatic dissemination once active disease is present.

evidence.reference_title: Alveolar echinococcosis: what triggers emergence in North America, Central Europe and Asia?
evidence.snippet: AE develops in a few healthy individuals, but preferentially in immunosuppressed patients.

nodes.description: E. multilocularis metacestodes grow as infiltrative, pseudotumoral intrahepatic masses, directly damaging liver parenchyma and resembling a malignant liver process.

evidence.snippet: Hepatic alveolar echinococcosis (HAE) is a rare but severe zoonosis caused by the pseudotumoral intrahepatic development of the larval stage of the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis.

evidence.reference_title: Hepatic alveolar hydatid disease (Echinococcus multilocularis), a mimic of liver malignancy: a review for the radiologist in non-endemic areas.
evidence.snippet: It is rare compared to cystic echinococcosis (CE), but like CE commonly affects the liver.

nodes.description: Infiltration of the liver hilum and central biliary structures can cause painless jaundice.

evidence.snippet: Painless jaundice is a sign of infiltration of the liver hilum and central biliary vessel involvement.

nodes.description: Excess late Th1/Th2 inflammation around the metacestode produces periparasitic fibrosis that can limit drug diffusion into the lesion.

evidence.reference_title: Chemotherapy for the treatment of alveolar echinococcosis: Where are we?
evidence.snippet: an excessive Th1/Th2 response, as observed in the late stage of the disease, is responsible for periparasitic fibrosis, limiting diffusion of drugs

nodes.description: Liver transplantation is a last-resort option for otherwise incurable AE with severe hepatic dysfunction, used only in carefully selected patients because immunosuppression can favor relapse or progression.

evidence.snippet: Liver transplantation is a last resort in patients of otherwise incurable disease.

nodes.description: Extrahepatic extension or hematogenous metastasis can involve neighboring organs or distant organs and is tracked in the N and M domains of PNM staging.

evidence.snippet: It describes the extension of the parasitic mass in the liver (P), the involvement of neighboring organs (N) and metastases (M)

nodes.description: E. multilocularis metacestodes induce a mixed periparasitic infiltrate of CD4-positive T cells, B cells, plasma cells, and macrophages, with regulatory T-cell signals such as FGL-2 dampening antiparasitic immunity.

evidence.reference_title: Chemotherapy for the treatment of alveolar echinococcosis: Where are we?
evidence.snippet: treatment with albendazole increases periparasite infiltration by immune cells (T CD4+ cells, B cells, plasmocytes, macrophages) and decreases the expression of FGL-2, a mediator secreted by T regulator cells (Tregs)

nodes.description: Advanced alveolar echinococcosis can produce portal hypertension through prehepatic, intrahepatic, or posthepatic vascular and biliary injury.

evidence.snippet: Alveolar echinococcosis-related portal hypertension can develop due to posthepatic pathology, intrahepatic pathology and prehepatic pathology.

nodes.description: Alveolar metacestodes appear as hepatic mass lesions with variable solid, cystic, necrotic, and calcified imaging components that can mimic malignancy.

evidence.snippet: Radiologically, alveolar echinococcosis manifestations are morphologically diverse and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of malignant and benign liver lesions.

nodes.description: The lung is the most common distant organ involved by hematogenous metastasis-like spread from hepatic AE.

evidence.snippet: Distant metastases are most common in the lung but can be found in every organ.

evidence.reference_title: Vascular pathology in patients with alveolar echinococcosis: framework for assessment and clinical management - a retrospective case series.
evidence.snippet: Distant metastases and/or extrahepatic manifestations were present in 16 patients (8.6%) with 14 cases of (7.5%) lung metastases.

nodes.description: Complete surgical excision of all AE lesions is the only curative treatment and is reserved for lesions in which an R0 resection is feasible; expert consensus pairs surgery with postoperative benzimidazole treatment.

evidence.snippet: Surgical treatment is the only treatment that can cure alveolar echinococcosis.
According to the current expert consensus, patients receive postoperative benzimidazole treatment for a duration of 2 years.

nodes.description: Recurrent obstruction of central bile ducts by AE strictures, debris, or necrotic-cavity communication drives secondary biliary injury.
nodes.id: Recurrent Biliary Obstruction and Secondary Biliary Sclerosis

evidence.snippet: Recurrent cholangitis, cholangiosepsis or liver abscess can occur even if alveolar echinococcosis-related stenoses of central bile ducts are treated with stenting and balloon dilation by repeated endoscopic retrograde cholangiography (ERC).

nodes.description: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiography with balloon dilatation or stenting is used to restore bile flow across AE-related central biliary stenoses.
nodes.id: Repeated ERCP with balloon dilatation or stenting

evidence.snippet: Biliary infiltration and obstruction are treated by repeated ERCP with balloon dilatation or stenting until bile flow is restored

nodes.description: Infiltration or compression of the portal vein, hepatic veins, or inferior vena cava can cause portal-vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari physiology, and portal hypertension.

evidence.snippet: Alveolar echinococcosis-related portal hypertension can develop due to posthepatic pathology, intrahepatic pathology and prehepatic pathology.
Alveolar echinococcosis-related infiltration of the hepatic segment of the inferior vena cava causes chronic Budd–Chiari syndrome and progressive damage to liver tissue and liver cirrhosis.
Alveolar echinococcosis-related infiltration or compression of the portal vein causes portal vein thrombosis, sometimes with cavernous portal vein transformation.

evidence.reference_title: Vascular pathology in patients with alveolar echinococcosis: framework for assessment and clinical management - a retrospective case series.
evidence.snippet: Over all 69 patients (37.1%) fulfilled radiological criteria for vascular involvement. PV was affected in 24.7% (45), HV in 22.6% (42), IVC in 13.4% (25) and HA in 5.9% (11).
